trial_name: ARREST — ECMO-facilitated Resuscitation for Refractory VF/VT OHCA (2020)
citation: Yannopoulos D, Bartos JA, Raveendran G, Walser E, Connett J, Murray TA, et al. Advanced reperfusion strategies for patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and refractory ventricular fibrillation (ARREST): a phase 2, single centre, open-label, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2020;396(10265):1807-1816
trial_type: RCT — single-centre, open-label, phase 2, pragmatic, Bayesian adaptive
one_liner: In a highly selected cohort with refractory VF/VT OHCA, an ECMO-facilitated resuscitation pathway increased survival to hospital discharge (43% vs 7%) compared to standard ACLS, but the trial was stopped early after 30 patients.

pico.population: Adults (18–75 years) with refractory VF/VT OHCA after ≥3 shocks, no sustained ROSC, mechanical CPR in use, and estimated transport time <30 minutes
pico.intervention: Early ECMO-facilitated resuscitation: immediate transfer to catheterisation lab for VA-ECMO and coronary angiography/PCI
pico.comparison: Standard ACLS in the emergency department without VA-ECMO capability

background.existing_knowledge: Adults with OHCA and persistent shockable rhythms after multiple defibrillations have very low survival with conventional ACLS. ECPR plus immediate coronary angiography/PCI had shown promising outcomes in observational cohorts, but confounding by selection and system factors limited causal inference.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether a protocolised ECMO-facilitated resuscitation strategy improves hard outcomes versus best conventional resuscitation, and whether benefits persist with acceptable neurological recovery.
background.hypothesis: In adults with refractory VF/VT OHCA meeting strict transport and device criteria, early ECMO-facilitated resuscitation increases survival to hospital discharge compared with continued standard ACLS.

methods.design: Phase 2, single-centre, open-label, pragmatic RCT with a hybrid Bayesian group-sequential design and response-adaptive randomisation. Randomisation occurred on hospital arrival.
methods.setting: An ECMO-capable centre within an integrated regional EMS system.

inclusion: Automated mechanical CPR device in use
exclusion: Sustained ROSC achieved within the first 3 shocks

methods.intervention: Early ECMO-facilitated resuscitation strategy: immediate transfer to the catheterisation laboratory for VA-ECMO initiation and coronary angiography/PCI, followed by protocolised ICU care.
methods.comparison: Standard ACLS strategy: continued conventional resuscitation in the emergency department without VA-ECMO capability. Patients achieving ROSC could proceed to standard post-arrest care and invasive coronary management.
methods.blinding: Open-label treatment assignment. Emergency teams were masked before randomisation; ICU team was masked to allocation; functional outcome assessors were blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: Simulated design targeted survival probabilities of 0.37 (ECMO) vs 0.12 (ACLS), with ~5% type I error and 90% power. Maximum sample size 150 evaluable outcomes (planned randomisation up to 174).
secondary_outcomes: Functional outcome (CPC and mRS) at discharge, 3 months, and 6 months
methods.follow_up: Survival to hospital discharge (primary) and survival/functional status to 3 and 6 months.

headline_bullets: Trial stopped early by DSMB after 30 patients due to efficacy (posterior probability of benefit 0.9861).
Survival to discharge was 43% (6/14) with early ECMO vs 7% (1/15) with standard ACLS.
At 6 months, all 6 survivors in the ECMO arm were alive with favourable neurological function (mean CPC 1.16); there were no survivors in the standard ACLS arm.
VA-ECMO was initiated in 80% (12/15) of the intervention arm; mean time from 911 call to ECMO initiation was 59 minutes.

outcomes_table.note: Primary outcome obtained in 29/30 (one early-ECMO patient withdrew on day 3).
No survivors in the standard ACLS arm beyond discharge except one in-hospital survivor (CPC 4, mRS 5).
Among survivors in the early ECMO arm: mean CPC 1.16 ± 0.4 (n=6) and mean mRS 1.3 ± 0.8 (n=6) at 6 months.
Cox model of survival time to death/discharge.
Two early-ECMO patients were pronounced dead due to severe metabolic derangements before cannulation.

outcomes_table.outcome: Access-site bleeding requiring >3 units PRBC (ICU subgroup)
outcomes_table.note: Complications reported among ICU admissions (early ECMO arm n=13; standard ACLS arm n=2).
No unanticipated device-related adverse events were reported.

safety: Access-site bleeding requiring >3 units PRBC: 2/13 (15%) in the early ECMO arm.
IVC trauma/retroperitoneal bleeding: 1/13 (8%) in the early ECMO arm.
No unanticipated device-related adverse events were reported.

domains.notes: Secure randomisation schedule using permuted blocks (sizes 2, 4, 6) with allocation concealed by a scratch-off opaque layer; emergency teams were masked before randomisation.
Open-label delivery is unavoidable; the primary endpoint (survival) is objective; ICU clinicians were masked to allocation; functional outcome assessment used blinded evaluators.

6/36 screened patients excluded pre-randomisation due to protocol misclassification; 30 randomised; 1/30 (early ECMO) withdrew consent on day 3 leading to missing primary outcome (primary endpoint analysed in 14 vs 15).

Early ECMO arm: all transferred to the catheterisation laboratory; VA-ECMO initiated in 12/15; 2/15 were declared dead due to severe metabolic derangements. Standard ACLS arm: VA-ECMO not available/used (0/15), with 2/15 transferred to the catheterisation laboratory after ROSC.
Groups were broadly similar for prehospital timings and characteristics; small imbalances (male sex 93.3% vs 73.3%) are difficult to interpret with n=30.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate: allocation concealment and objective primary outcome support credibility, but early stopping, small sample size, open-label delivery, and one missing primary endpoint meaningfully limit precision and robustness.

domains.notes: Highly selected cohort (18–75 years, refractory VF/VT after 3 shocks, mechanical CPR in use, and estimated transport time <30 minutes) within a specialised regional system; excludes non-shockable rhythms and longer transport/low-resource contexts.

Findings are tightly coupled to a coordinated EMS-to-cath-lab pathway with immediate access to VA-ECMO cannulation and coronary intervention; many systems cannot replicate time-to-cannulation (mean 59 minutes from 911 call). The tested strategy is a bundled pathway, so translation requires reproducing the bundle rather than adopting a single component.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is limited: results best generalise to mature ECPR-capable systems with short low-flow times and strict selection for refractory shockable OHCA.

strengths: Randomised evaluation of an ECPR-based system-of-care.
Blinded ICU team and blinded functional outcome assessors.
limitations: Early stopping at first interim analysis.
One withdrawal leading to missing primary outcome.
Comparator reflects ED-based ACLS without ECPR access and may not represent the best achievable conventional strategy in all regions.
Adverse event comparisons are hard to interpret because most standard-arm patients died before ICU admission.

critical_appraisal.summary: A small, single-centre RCT with a large effect size but wide uncertainty due to early termination, providing proof-of-concept for an ECMO-facilitated system-of-care in highly selected refractory shockable OHCA.
strengths: Randomised design with concealed allocation and objective primary outcome.
Clear separation of the intervention bundle from standard care.
weaknesses: Early termination at first interim analysis inflates risk of effect-size overestimation.
Small sample size (n=30) yields imprecise estimates.

sections.authors_conclusion: In a rigorously selected refractory VF/VT OHCA cohort, the early ECMO strategy was associated with substantially higher survival to discharge and preserved 6-month survival, with favourable functional outcomes among survivors.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial supports the plausibility of benefit for ECPR in refractory shockable OHCA when systems can deliver rapid cannulation and invasive management; it does not justify indiscriminate ECPR expansion.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Highly selected patients (18-75 years, refractory VF/VT, mechanical CPR, short transport) treated in mature, high-volume ECPR-capable systems.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: ECPR is superior to standard ACLS in all OHCA patients or that ECMO alone is the key driver of benefit.
implementation_caveats: Requires reproducing the entire system bundle (prehospital triage, mechanical CPR, rapid transport, 24/7 cath lab + ECMO team).
Mean time from 911 call to ECMO initiation was 59 minutes, a benchmark that may be difficult to achieve in many settings.

controversies.notes: Correspondence argued that randomising on hospital arrival (mean 48.5 minutes from 911 call) may not optimally capture the time-sensitive biology of ECPR, suggesting earlier triage/randomisation could be important.

controversies.topic: Early stopping and small-sample inferential fragility
controversies.notes: Termination after 30 participants raises the likelihood of effect-size inflation and leaves wide uncertainty (95% credible interval for the primary risk difference 3.7 to 59.2).
The intervention combines ECPR with immediate invasive coronary evaluation and highly organised logistics; causal attribution to VA-ECMO alone is not supported by the design.

context_related_trials.relation: A subsequent multicentre RCT that did not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in 30-day survival with favourable neurological outcome (20% vs 16%; OR 1.4; 95% CI 0.5 to 3.5; P=0.52), and excluded 26/160 after randomisation, emphasising practical challenges of strict selection and delivery fidelity at scale.
An individual patient data pooled analysis combining ARREST and PRAGUE OHCA data explored how patient selection and low-flow times may modify benefit.

unresolved_questions: Can the results be replicated in a multicentre, larger-scale RCT?
What is the optimal timing for randomisation and ECMO initiation?
What are the independent contributions of ECMO vs. early coronary angiography to the observed benefit?

numbers_to_remember: Mean time 911 call to ECMO: 59 minutes
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: A bundled ECMO-facilitated resuscitation pathway can dramatically improve survival in highly selected refractory VF/VT OHCA, but only in systems that can replicate its rapid timelines and strict patient selection.
